Chapter Six: Building Coalitions—The Promise and Peril of Unity
Coalition-building—it sounds pretty straightforward, right? Just people from different backgrounds coming together for a shared goal.
But in real life, it’s more like a delicate dance, full of both hope and heartbreak. After those first big wins for women’s suffrage, organizations tried to bridge some serious divides—race, class, even clashing ideas about what real progress looked like.
Sometimes, these efforts sparked real, lasting change. But other times? They only made it painfully clear how deep those old wounds still ran.
Imagine walking into a busy community center in a northern city. Women from every walk of life are gathered, planning a campaign for better housing. There’s laughter in the air, but you can almost feel the tension, too. Some women worry their voices will get lost, that their needs might be overlooked. Others are determined to find some common ground—to build something bigger than just themselves. The room buzzes with possibility, but you can also sense the heavy weight of history.
Take the National Association of Colored Women’s Clubs, for example. They became a real powerhouse by bringing Black women together from all corners of the country. Their motto—“Lifting as we climb”—says it all. These clubs didn’t just talk about progress; they rolled up their sleeves and got to work, tackling everything from education to anti-lynching campaigns. They showed the world what’s possible when women refuse to be divided.
But even as these coalitions started forming, the mainstream women’s movement often struggled to include everyone, truly and fully. Sometimes, white-led organizations would invite Black women to join—but only if it was on their own terms. And when conflicts came up, it was often women of color whose voices got pushed to the side, or silenced completely. The dream of unity was real, but so were the barriers.
People soon realized that building strong, lasting coalitions took more than just good intentions. It meant really listening—being willing to share power, and having the courage to face some tough, uncomfortable truths. Many learned these lessons the hard way—through alliances that fell apart, betrayals that hurt deeply, and the long, slow work of rebuilding trust.
Yet, even with all the setbacks, the dream of solidarity never faded away. In times of crisis, women found ways to show up for each other—to support one another when it mattered most. These moments, even if they were brief, left a mark.
They proved that unity is possible—but only if every single voice is heard.
